module_title: Getting Started with Dried Fruit & Vegetable Business

lessons.title: Why Drying Food is a Smart Business in Africa
lessons.body: Drying food is one of the oldest and smartest businesses in Africa. Every year, farmers lose up to 40% of their harvest because they cannot eat or sell it fast enough. Tomatoes, mangoes, and leafy greens rot within days. But when you dry them, they last for months. That means you can buy cheap during harvest season and sell when prices are high. For example, a crate of tomatoes costs 5,000 Naira in Nigeria during peak season, but dried tomato flakes can sell for 15,000 Naira per kilogram year-round. The profit margin is huge because drying removes water, so 10 kg of fresh tomatoes become about 1 kg of dried product. You also solve a real problem: people in cities want healthy, natural snacks without preservatives. Dried mango, pineapple, and banana chips are in high demand in supermarkets, schools, and bus parks. Unlike fresh fruit, dried products don't need refrigeration, so you can transport them to distant markets without spoilage. Starting a drying business requires very little capital. You can begin with a solar dryer made from wood and polythene, or even sun-drying on clean mats. The main costs are raw materials, packaging, and your time. With consistent quality, you can supply local shops, hotels, and even export to Africans in the diaspora who miss home foods. The business is also climate-smart: you use the sun, a free resource, and reduce waste. Many successful African entrepreneurs started exactly this wayâdrying one product, then expanding. So if you want a low-risk, high-demand business that turns perishable crops into lasting wealth, drying is your answer.

lessons.title: Identifying Local Fruits and Vegetables for Drying
lessons.body: Not all fruits and vegetables dry well. You need produce with high sugar or low water content, and firm texture. In Africa, the best fruits for drying include mangoes, pineapples, bananas, papayas, guavas, and jackfruit. These have natural sweetness and hold their shape after drying. Avoid watery fruits like watermelon or orangesâthey turn to mush. For vegetables, good choices are tomatoes, onions, peppers, okra, leafy greens (like spinach, kale, and amaranth), carrots, and pumpkin. Leafy greens dry quickly and become nutritious powders for soups. Tomatoes and peppers dry into flakes or powder for stews. Okra dries into chips or powder for soups. When selecting produce, choose ripe but firm fruits. Overripe fruits are mushy and may ferment; underripe ones lack flavor. Buy from local farmers during harvest when prices are lowest. For example, in Kenya, mangoes are abundant in January and February, so you can buy a bucket for 100 KES. In West Africa, tomatoes are cheapest in the dry season. Always inspect for bruises, mold, or insect damageâthese spoil the batch. Wash everything thoroughly in clean water, then cut into uniform slices (3-5 mm thick) for even drying. Remove seeds from peppers and tomatoes if you want powder. For bananas and plantains, peel and slice. Some fruits like apples and pears brown quickly; dip them in lemon juice or salt water for 5 minutes before drying. Remember, the goal is to preserve local, seasonal abundance. You can also dry herbs like mint, basil, and moringa. Moringa leaves are highly nutritious and sell well as powder. Start with one or two products you can source easily and consistently, then add more as you learn.

lessons.title: Setting Up a Small-Scale Drying Workspace at Home
lessons.body: You don't need a factory to start drying food. A clean, well-ventilated space at home is enough. Choose a room or covered area away from dust, smoke, and animals. If you have a kitchen with a window, that works. For sun-drying, you need direct sunlight for at least 6-8 hours a day. A concrete slab, a raised wooden platform, or a table covered with clean mesh works well. Never dry food directly on the groundâdirt and insects will contaminate it. For solar drying, you can build a simple cabinet dryer using wood, a clear polythene sheet or glass, and a black-painted metal sheet as a heat absorber. Place it facing the sun. The black sheet absorbs heat, and air enters from bottom vents and exits from top vents, carrying moisture away. This protects food from rain, dust, and flies. Your workspace must have good air circulation. If the air is stagnant, food won't dry and may mold. Also, keep the area dry and free of standing water. For safety, store your tools and packaging materials on shelves, not on the floor. If you have pets, keep them out. A small table for cutting and weighing, a sink or basin for washing, and a drying rack are the main zones. You can start with a 1m x 1m drying rack that holds about 5 kg of fresh produce. As you grow, add more racks or build a larger solar dryer. Remember, cleanliness is critical: wash your hands, wear clean aprons, and sanitize surfaces before handling food. A simple setup like this can produce 20-30 kg of dried product per month, enough to test the market and earn extra income.

lessons.title: Basic Tools and Equipment You Need to Start
lessons.body: To start a dried fruit and vegetable business, you need only a few affordable tools. First, a sharp stainless steel knife and a cutting board. Stainless steel doesn't rust or react with food. A good knife costs about 2,000-5,000 Naira or 500-1,000 KES. Next, you need drying trays. These can be made from wooden frames with food-grade mesh (like mosquito netting or stainless steel mesh). Avoid using wire mesh that rusts. You can make 10 trays for under 10,000 Naira. For solar drying, you'll need a clear polythene sheet (UV-treated) or glass, and black paint for the heat absorber. A simple solar dryer can be built for 20,000-50,000 Naira. If you prefer electric drying, a small food dehydrator costs 50,000-150,000 Naira, but it uses electricity. For packaging, you need airtight containers or sealed bags. A impulse sealer (for plastic bags) costs around 15,000 Naira. You also need a weighing scale (digital, 5-10 kg capacity) to measure products for sale. A scale costs 10,000-20,000 Naira. Other useful items: a large basin for washing, a colander, a peeler, a blender (for powder), and clean cloths or paper towels. For safety, get gloves, hairnets, and aprons. You can start with a total budget of 50,000-100,000 Naira (about $60-$120). Many of these items you may already have. Don't buy everything at once; start with the basics and reinvest profits. For example, use sun-drying on mesh trays initially, then upgrade to a solar dryer after your first sales. Always buy food-grade materialsânever use old fertilizer bags or non-food plastic for packaging.

lessons.title: Understanding Costs and Setting Your First Prices
lessons.body: To make a profit, you must know your costs. Let's break down a simple example: drying 10 kg of fresh mangoes. In many African markets, 10 kg of mangoes cost about 2,000 Naira (or 200 KES). After peeling and slicing, you get about 8 kg of usable fruit. Drying removes about 80-90% of water, so you end up with 1-1.5 kg of dried mango. If you sell dried mango at 5,000 Naira per kg, your revenue is 5,000-7,500 Naira. Your costs include: raw materials (2,000), packaging (500 for bags and labels), and maybe transport (500). Total costs = 3,000 Naira. Profit = 2,000-4,500 Naira. That's a 40-60% margin. But you must also factor in your time and equipment depreciation. If you dry 10 batches per month, you can earn 20,000-45,000 Naira profit. To set your price, check what competitors charge. Visit local markets, supermarkets, and online (Jumia, Kilimall). If dried mango sells for 6,000 Naira per kg, price yours at 5,500 to attract customers while still making profit. For vegetables like dried tomatoes, a kg of fresh tomatoes costs 500 Naira, yields about 100g dried, which sells for 2,000-3,000 Naira per kg. So 10 kg fresh (5,000 Naira) yields 1 kg dried (2,000-3,000 Naira)âthat's a loss if you only sell 1 kg. So you need to dry larger quantities or add value (e.g., tomato powder blends). Always calculate your yield ratio: for every 10 kg fresh, you get 1-1.5 kg dried. Price accordingly. Start with small batches, track every expense, and adjust. Offer samples to build trust. As your brand grows, you can charge premium prices for organic or well-packaged products.

lessons.title: Health and Safety Rules for Handling Food
lessons.body: Food safety is non-negotiable. If your dried products make someone sick, your business is finished. Always follow these rules. First, personal hygiene: wash your hands with soap and clean water before touching food, after using the toilet, and after handling waste. Wear clean clothes, an apron, and a hairnet. Keep fingernails short and clean. If you are sick, especially with diarrhea or vomiting, do not handle food. Second, clean and sanitize all surfaces, knives, and trays before and after use. Use hot water and food-safe sanitizer, or a mixture of vinegar and water. Third, wash all fruits and vegetables thoroughly in clean running water. For leafy greens, soak in salt water for 10 minutes to remove insects, then rinse. Fourth, dry food properly. Incomplete drying leads to mold, which produces dangerous toxins. To test dryness: fruits should be leathery with no moist spots; vegetables should be brittle. If you bend a dried tomato, it should snap, not bend. Fifth, store dried products in airtight containers in a cool, dark, dry place. Moisture is the enemy. Add a small oxygen absorber or silica gel packet to prevent mold. Sixth, protect from pests: use sealed containers, keep the workspace clean, and avoid leaving food exposed. Seventh, label your products with the production date and best-before date (usually 6-12 months). Finally, never mix spoiled produce with good ones. If you see mold, throw away the entire batchâdo not try to salvage it. Following these rules ensures your products are safe, and customers will trust your brand. You can also take a free online food safety course for more details.

lessons.title: Practical Reference
lessons.body:
Practical Reference: Getting Started with Dried Fruit & Vegetable Business

This practical reference consolidates the essentials from the six opening lessons of the Dried Fruit & Vegetable Processing module. It is written for African entrepreneurs who want to move from "I have surplus produce" to "I have a sellable, safe, profitable dried food product." Use it as your field manual: print it, pin it in your workspace, and refer to it each time you start a new batch or price a new product.

1. Why Drying Food Is a Smart Business in Africa

Africa loses an estimated 30â40% of its fresh fruit and vegetable harvest after production, largely due to poor storage, weak cold chains, and market gluts during peak season. Drying converts that waste into value: it reduces weight by 70â90%, extends shelf life from days to months, removes the need for refrigeration, and lets you sell when prices are higher. For a small operator, drying is one of the lowest-capital food processing businesses you can enter â you can start with a solar dryer, a few trays, and one reliable supplier of raw material.

Business-first framing: drying is not just preservation, it is arbitrage. You buy mangoes at 500â1,000 TZS/kg in season and sell dried mango slices at 8,000â15,000 TZS/kg year-round. The margin comes from time-shifting supply and reducing transport weight. Your job is to protect that margin with consistent quality, safe handling, and reliable packaging.

2. Identifying Local Fruits and Vegetables for Drying

Not every crop dries well. The best candidates are high in sugar or fibre, hold colour and flavour after drying, and are available in surplus. In most African markets, the strongest starting crops are mango, pineapple, banana, tomato, onion, okra, leafy greens (collards, amaranth, moringa), and hot pepper. Start with one or two crops you can source cheaply and consistently before adding more.

Table 1: Suitability of common African crops for small-scale drying
Crop Drying suitability Typical dry yield (from 1 kg fresh) Best use / market
MangoExcellent150â200 gSnack slices, export
PineappleExcellent120â180 gSnack, confectionery
BananaVery good250â300 gSnack, flour
TomatoVery good60â100 gSauces, soups, seasoning
OnionVery good100â150 gSeasoning, spice blends
OkraGood100â150 gSnack, soup thickener
Leafy greens (moringa, amaranth)Good (shade-dry)80â120 gNutrition powder
Hot pepperExcellent150â250 gSpice, condiment

Sources: FAO Traditional Food Processing and Solar Drying of Fruits and Vegetables technical notes; yield ranges are indicative and vary with variety, maturity, and drying method.

3. Setting Up a Small-Scale Drying Workspace at Home

You do not need a factory. You need a clean, ventilated, pest-free space with three zones: a preparation area (wash, peel, slice), a drying area (solar dryer or dehydrator), and a packaging and storage area (dry, dark, sealed). Keep the zones separate to prevent cross-contamination. Site the dryer on a raised platform facing the midday sun, with clearance for airflow. Store finished product off the floor in sealed containers with a moisture absorber if available.

4. Basic Tools and Equipment You Need to Start

Your first kit should cost less than the value of one good harvest. Prioritise stainless steel or food-grade plastic, because reactive metals (iron, copper) discolour food and speed up spoilage.

Table 2: Starter equipment list and indicative cost range (East Africa, 2024)
Item Purpose Indicative cost (USD) Priority
Solar dryer (cabinet or tunnel)Controlled drying80â400Essential
Stainless steel knives & cutting boardsPrep15â40Essential
Food-grade drying traysLoading product10â30Essential
Digital thermometer / hygrometerMonitor temperature & humidity10â25Essential
Kitchen scale (0.1 gâ5 kg)Yield & pricing records15â35Essential
Sealer or vacuum bagsPackaging & shelf life30â150Important
Blanching pot & colanderPretreatment10â25Important
Hygiene kit (soap, gloves, hairnets, sanitiser)Food safety10â20Essential

Sources: Indicative prices compiled from East African agri-input suppliers and FAO small-scale food processing equipment guides (2024). Actual prices vary by country and supplier.

5. Understanding Costs and Setting Your First Prices

Price from cost, not from guesswork. Add every input: raw material, labour, energy, packaging, transport, spoilage, and a margin for reinvestment. A simple formula:

Selling price per kg = (Total batch cost Ã· Dry kg produced) Ã (1 + Target margin %)

Example: 20 kg fresh mango at 800 TZS/kg = 16,000 TZS. Labour, energy, packaging = 9,000 TZS. Total = 25,000 TZS. Dry yield at 18% = 3.6 kg. Cost per dry kg = 6,944 TZS. At a 60% margin, sell at ~11,100 TZS/kg. Track every batch â your records are your pricing power.

â ï¸ SAFETY WARNING â FOOD SAFETY IS NON-NEGOTIABLE

Never sell dried food that shows mould, off-smell, sliminess, or insect damage. Aflatoxin and other mycotoxins from poorly dried or stored produce can cause liver cancer and are not destroyed by cooking. Dry thoroughly (target <15% moisture for most fruits, <10% for vegetables), cool completely before packing, use clean water, wash hands, and keep raw and dried product separate. If in doubt, throw the batch out â one bad batch can destroy your brand and harm your community.

6. Health and Safety Rules for Handling Food

  • Wash hands with soap before and after every stage; wear clean aprons, hairnets, and gloves.
  • Use only clean, potable water for washing and blanching.
  • Keep animals, pests, and unauthorised people out of the drying and packing areas.
  • Dry at the correct temperature (50â60Â°C for most fruits and vegetables); avoid open-air drying where dust and flies are present.
  • Cool dried product fully before sealing to prevent condensation and mould.
  • Label every batch with product name, date, and weight; keep records for traceability.
  • Store in food-grade, airtight containers away from sunlight, moisture, and chemicals.

Quick Reference Checklist

  1. Source raw material in season at the lowest reliable price; reject spoiled pieces.
  2. Wash, peel, and slice uniformly â uniform size dries evenly.
  3. Pretreat (blanch or lemon-juice dip) to protect colour and nutrients.
  4. Load trays with space between pieces; do not overcrowd.
  5. Dry at 50â60Â°C until leathery or brittle, not sticky.
  6. Cool completely, then pack in sealed, labelled food-grade containers.
  7. Record weight in, weight out, drying time, and batch cost.
  8. Price from full cost plus margin; review prices every season.

Further Reading (Free Official Resources)

  • FAO â Food Loss and Food Waste: data and guides on post-harvest losses and value addition.
  • FAO â Small-Scale Fruit and Vegetable Processing: practical processing and drying methods.
  • WHO â Five Keys to Safer Food: essential food safety rules for any food business.
  • Codex Alimentarius â Codes of Practice: international hygiene and processing standards.
  • IFAD â Rural Development and Agribusiness: financing and market access for small processors.

Prepared for the RISE AFRICA Skills programme, Dried Fruit & Vegetable Processing module. Always verify local regulations and market prices before launching.

quiz.q: What percentage of Africa's harvest is typically lost due to spoilage?
quiz.explanation: The lesson states that farmers lose up to 40% of their harvest due to spoilage.

quiz.q: Which of these fruits is NOT recommended for drying?
quiz.explanation: Watermelon has high water content and turns to mush when dried.

quiz.q: What is a key advantage of dried products over fresh produce?
options: B) They last for months without refrigeration
quiz.explanation: Dried products can be stored for months without refrigeration, unlike fresh produce.

quiz.q: When buying produce for drying, you should choose fruits that are:
quiz.explanation: Ripe but firm fruits have good flavor and hold their shape during drying.

quiz.q: Why should you avoid drying food directly on the ground?
options: B) It attracts insects and dirt
quiz.explanation: Ground drying exposes food to dirt, insects, and contamination.

quiz.q: What is a solar dryer made of?
options: A) Wood, clear polythene, and black metal sheet
quiz.explanation: A simple solar dryer uses wood for frame, clear cover, and black absorber.

quiz.q: How much fresh produce can a 1m x 1m drying rack hold?
quiz.explanation: The lesson states a 1m x 1m rack holds about 5 kg of fresh produce.

quiz.q: Which tool is essential for packaging dried products?
quiz.explanation: An impulse sealer is used to seal plastic bags airtight.

quiz.q: What is the approximate cost of a digital weighing scale for a small business?
quiz.explanation: The lesson mentions a digital scale costs 10,000-20,000 Naira.

quiz.q: Why should you avoid using old fertilizer bags for packaging?
options: B) They are not food-grade and can contaminate
quiz.explanation: Fertilizer bags contain chemicals that can leach into food.

quiz.q: In the cost example, 10 kg of fresh mangoes cost how much?
quiz.explanation: The lesson states 10 kg of mangoes cost about 2,000 Naira.

quiz.q: What is the typical yield of dried product from 10 kg of fresh mangoes?
quiz.explanation: Drying removes water, leaving about 1-1.5 kg from 10 kg fresh.

quiz.q: If dried mango sells for 5,000 Naira per kg, what is the revenue from 1.5 kg?
quiz.explanation: 1.5 kg multiplied by 5,000 Naira equals 7,500 Naira.

quiz.q: Why is it important to calculate your yield ratio?
options: A) To know how much water to add
B) To set prices that cover costs and yield profit
quiz.explanation: Yield ratio helps you understand how much dried product you get and price accordingly.

quiz.q: Which of these is a fixed cost in a drying business?
quiz.explanation: Equipment depreciation is a fixed cost, while others are variable.

quiz.q: What should you do before touching food?
quiz.explanation: Handwashing with soap is the first rule of food safety.

quiz.q: How can you test if dried vegetables are properly dried?
options: B) They should be brittle and snap
quiz.explanation: Properly dried vegetables are brittle and snap when bent.

quiz.q: What is a sign of incomplete drying?
quiz.explanation: Mold indicates moisture remains, which is unsafe.

quiz.q: Where should you store dried products?
options: B) In a cool, dark, dry place
quiz.explanation: Cool, dark, dry conditions prevent spoilage and maintain quality.

quiz.q: What can you add to packaging to prevent mold?
options: B) Oxygen absorber or silica gel
quiz.explanation: Oxygen absorbers or silica gel reduce moisture and oxygen, preventing mold.

quiz.q: What should you do if you find mold on a batch of dried fruit?
options: A) Cut off the moldy part and sell the rest
B) Throw away the entire batch
quiz.explanation: Mold produces toxins that spread, so the whole batch must be discarded.

quiz.q: Why is food safety important for your business?
options: A) It makes food taste better
B) It builds customer trust and avoids legal issues
quiz.explanation: Safe food builds trust and prevents illness, protecting your reputation.

quiz.q: Which of these is a good source of information on food safety?
quiz.explanation: Free online courses provide reliable food safety training.

quiz.q: What is the recommended thickness for slicing fruits for drying?
quiz.explanation: Uniform 3-5 mm slices dry evenly.

quiz.q: Why should you dip apples or pears in lemon juice before drying?
quiz.explanation: Lemon juice (acid) prevents enzymatic browning.

quiz.q: What is moringa commonly dried into?
quiz.explanation: Moringa leaves are dried and ground into a nutritious powder.

quiz.q: Which of these is a good vegetable for drying?
quiz.explanation: Tomatoes dry well into flakes or powder; cucumber and lettuce are too watery.

quiz.q: What is the first step in setting up a drying workspace?
options: B) Choose a clean, well-ventilated area
quiz.explanation: A clean, ventilated space is the foundation for safe drying.

quiz.q: Why is air circulation important in a drying workspace?
options: B) It helps remove moisture and prevents mold
D) It makes food dry faster
quiz.explanation: Good air circulation carries moisture away, preventing mold growth.

quiz.q: What is a simple way to protect drying food from flies and dust?
options: A) Use a solar dryer or mesh cover
quiz.explanation: A solar dryer or mesh cover keeps flies and dust off the food.
